identification: Agriculture Victoria describes the European rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus) as a small leporid with long hind legs, short front legs, long ears and side-set eyes. Adults usually weigh 0.8-2.3 kg. The coat is typically grey-brown with a pale belly. Black or ginger animals are under 2 percent, and white animals are rarely seen. Juveniles often have a white forehead star that is lost at the three-month moult. Bucks, does and kittens are the usual names for males, females and young. Rabbits and hares are the only local mammals with a second pair of upper incisors (peg teeth) behind the gnawing pair, and that tooth row leaves a 45-degree cut on browsed plants. They are most active from dusk until dawn, live in social groups, and use a home range of about 0.2-2 ha. The warren is essential for breeding because newborn rabbits (about 35 g) cannot survive temperature extremes without it. They also use fallen timber, rocks, dense scrub, woody weeds and debris, and they will live around houses, farm buildings and water tanks. A running rabbit holds the tail up so the underside looks white. Source: https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/biosecurity/pest-animals/established-pest-animal-species/european-rabbit (page last updated 15 Jan 2025).
origins: Agriculture Victoria gives the origin as southern France and Spain. Domestic breeds came with early European settlement. The first wild populations reported in Australia were in Tasmania in the early 1800s. They did not establish on the mainland until 1859, when Thomas Austin released at least 13 wild rabbits at Barwon Park near Geelong. Seven years later more than 14,000 rabbits had been shot on that estate. By the 1920s rabbits occupied most of the southern half of Australia. Spread is given as 10-15 km a year in wet forest and over 100 km a year in the rangelands, described as the fastest colonisation by any mammal. Barwon Park is introduction history near Geelong. It is not an Inverleigh record and is not used here as a local hangout. Source: https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/biosecurity/pest-animals/established-pest-animal-species/european-rabbit.
impacts: The same Agriculture Victoria page says at least 304 Australian threatened fauna and flora species are affected by competition and land degradation by rabbits, and that this is listed as a key threatening process under the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999. Selective feeding at seeding and seedling stages stops regeneration, can cause soil erosion, and can favour noxious or unpalatable weeds. The page links high rabbit numbers to the disappearance of the greater bilby and the pig-footed bandicoot and says research in semi-arid sites found that less than one rabbit per hectare can severely damage some plants. Rabbits compete with native wildlife for food and habitat. They also hold up numbers of cats and foxes, and the page says those predators press harder on native animals when rabbit numbers crash, so foxes should be controlled before rabbit control. The impact section estimates over $200 million a year in lost Australian agricultural production, and $30 million a year for beef, lamb and wool in Victoria and Tasmania alone. A video transcript on the same page says more than $200 million in lost production and that seven rabbits equal one dry sheep equivalent. Those are national and industry figures, not an Inverleigh measurement. No diet or damage study from Inverleigh was found. Local evidence is the occurrence rows and remarks: droppings, scratchings and diggings at Inverleigh coordinates, and rabbit holes near a creek on a Bannockburn observation. Source: https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/biosecurity/pest-animals/established-pest-animal-species/european-rabbit.

whatToDo: Report rabbit sightings, warrens, damage and control to FeralScan. ALA stores the local mass of records as dataResourceName FeralScan and datasetName rabbitScan, so new reports go into the same public program (https://www.feralscan.org.au/). The FeralScan site returned only an application shell to this client, so button-level steps are not copied from it. On the land, Agriculture Victoria's rabbit page and its video describe an integrated sequence they call the Rabbit Recipe: monitor and coordinate with neighbours; reduce numbers (the page says baiting is the usual reduction step); destroy harbour by ripping warrens and, where applicable, removing above-ground shelter; follow up by re-ripping or fumigating reopenings; keep monitoring. The video says the useful seasons are the summer break for baiting when other feed is scarce, ripping straight after that while soils are friable, and fumigation as follow-up in autumn and winter. This file does not give bait rates, fumigant rates or poison recipes. Follow the Agriculture Victoria method pages and the product label. The rabbit species page says to control foxes before rabbit control, because predators press harder on native animals when rabbit numbers crash. The integrated fox control page, not the rabbit species page, is where this pass read the warning that native wildlife may use the same harbour and that council, DEECA, Aboriginal Affairs Victoria or the Registered Aboriginal Party, and the catchment authority should be asked before works disturb native vegetation, culturally significant areas or waterways. That caution applies to ripping and harbour removal as well. No Corangamite CMA page opened in this pass gave a local rabbit count or a site prescription. Myxoma virus and RHDV already circulate and the page says they hold rabbits to about 15 percent of potential numbers. They are not a reason to skip warren removal. identification: Agriculture Victoria: only the red fox (Vulpes vulpes) occurs in Australia, of 21 fox species worldwide. Big ears, bushy tail, usually reddish-brown above, whitish or grey chin, chest and belly. The tail tip is often white and sometimes black or dark red. Narrow chest, long legs, and long high-set semi-retractable claws. Males typically 4-8 kg, females 4-6 kg. Mostly nocturnal, travelling 10-15 km a night, and resting by day in hollow logs or trees, enlarged rabbit burrows or dense undergrowth. Where rabbits are present they make up the bulk of the diet. Other foods listed are carrion, house mice, insects, reptiles, amphibians, birds, grain, vegetable matter and fruit. Most prey weighs 35-5500 g. Foxes cache food and will surplus-kill. The species page and the video transcript disagree about Tasmania: the page says foxes have been reported in Tasmania, and the video says they are in all states and territories except Tasmania. Both texts are on Agriculture Victoria pages. Source: https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/biosecurity/pest-animals/established-pest-animal-species/red-fox.
origins: Origin Europe. Introduced for hunting in the mid-1850s, with most releases around Melbourne. About 20 years later they were declared a pest in Victoria. Within 100 years they had reached their current mainland distribution. The page says they now occur over 75 percent of Australia and that the range is strongly linked with rabbits. Victorian habitats listed include urban areas, alpine heaths, rainforests, coasts and the Mallee. Densities given are as many as 16 per km2 in Melbourne and about 4-8 per km2 in temperate agricultural land. Those figures are not Inverleigh densities. Source: https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/biosecurity/pest-animals/established-pest-animal-species/red-fox.
impacts: The red fox species page says fox predation is a key threatening process under the Endangered Species Protection Act 1992 and the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999. It names a threat to at least 14 bird, 48 mammal, 12 reptile and two amphibian species, and says almost any animal up to 5.5 kg is at risk. A single fox is estimated to eat about 400 g a night, about 150 kg a year, and may kill far more than it eats. The page's economic estimate is about $227.5 million a year for Australia, split on that page as $17.5 million sheep production, $190 million environmental impacts, $16 million management and $4 million research. Primary predation is given as a possible 4-30 percent of lamb loss, and the page says the production impact is still largely unquantified. The integrated fox control page gives a different 2020-21 figure: about $198 million in lost production. The video transcript on both pages repeats $227.5 million a year. The two dollar figures are left side by side. Foxes also move weed seeds (boxthorn, sweet briar and blackberry are named). Diseases listed as transmissible to dogs or people include sarcoptic mange, hydatids and leptospirosis. Rabies is discussed only as a potential future risk. No Inverleigh diet study was found. The local rows show foxes in the Inverleigh reserve and common, including one animal moving into 'A paradoxa', and foxes at Bannockburn including a scat-analysis record and a fox immediately followed by a hare. Sources: https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/biosecurity/pest-animals/established-pest-animal-species/red-fox ; https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/biosecurity/pest-animals/invasive-animal-management/integrated-fox-control.
legalStatus: Declared established pest animal under the Catchment and Land Protection Act 1994. Landowners must take all reasonable steps to prevent the spread of, and as far as possible eradicate, established pest animals (CaLP Act s.20(1)(f), as quoted on the established-invasive-animals page). Integrated fox control repeats that duty. Agriculture Victoria also publishes a Victorian Fox Bounty page. That page returned HTTP 403 in this pass, so the current payment, dates and collection rules are not stated here. identification: Agriculture Victoria uses European hare, Lepus europaeus. Adults about 3.5-5.0 kg, males generally smaller than females. Ears extend past the nose when held forward. Hind legs longer than the front. Flecked tan, black and white fur, ruddy brown or grey above and white below. Twenty-eight teeth, with the same double upper incisors as rabbits and the same 45-degree cut on browse. Hares run with the tail down and it looks black. Rabbits run with the tail up and it looks white. The hare iris is light brown, with a clear pupil. They are solitary, rest in a shallow form about 400 by 200 mm rather than a warren, and are born furred with eyes open. Home range averages about 149 ha. They travel 3-4 km to feed and can sprint to about 50 km/h. Source: https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/biosecurity/pest-animals/established-pest-animal-species/european-hare (page last updated 15 Jan 2025).
origins: Origin on the Agriculture Victoria page: Europe and Central Asia. First wild populations in Australia on the shores of Westernport Bay in 1862. In 1863 the Acclimatisation Society of Victoria established a colony on Phillip Island for coursing. By 1870 they were widespread in south-eastern Australia, spreading at about 60 km a year. They had crossed the Murray by 1875 and reached the Queensland border by 1900. The page says they became a major agricultural problem in northern and western Victoria and occupy about 700,000 km2. They are widespread in open grassland, woodland, agricultural and urban areas in Victoria. The Australian Faunal Directory distribution note for the accepted concept Lepus capensis is 'Introduced from Europe.' Westernport Bay and Phillip Island are introduction history, not Inverleigh hangouts. Sources: https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/biosecurity/pest-animals/established-pest-animal-species/european-hare ; https://biodiversity.org.au/afd/taxa/Lepus_capensis.
impacts: Agriculture Victoria: hares gnaw bark and chew stems of young trees and shrubs, which is a particular problem at revegetation sites. They graze grasses and also vegetables, lucerne and cereals, and they ringbark young trees and vines in forestry, ornamental and fruit plantings. One animal can travel far enough to damage plants over a wide area. Predators listed are foxes, feral and domestic cats, feral and domestic pigs, dingoes, quolls, goannas and wedge-tailed eagles. RHDV2 can kill hares. The page says RHDV1 K5 has not been shown to affect anything but rabbits. No Inverleigh damage study was found. The local remarks are animals moving between the Inverleigh golf course and the nature reserve, on Links track on the common, two together in grassland at Teesdale Grassy Woodland Reserve, and a hare immediately after a fox on a Bannockburn powerline track.
legalStatus: European hares are declared established pest animals in Victoria under the Catchment and Land Protection Act 1994. They are in the established-invasive-animals list with rabbits, so the landowner duty in section 20(1)(f) applies: all reasonable steps to prevent the spread and, as far as possible, eradicate them on the land. Sources: https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/biosecurity/pest-animals/established-pest-animal-species/european-hare ; https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/biosecurity/pest-animals/invasive-animal-management/established-invasive-animals.

identification: The Australian Museum: despite the name, the black rat is usually brown or grey. Yellow-enamel chisel incisors separate rats from carnivorous marsupials such as antechinus. Long pointed head (rounder in juveniles). Large thin ears, 20 mm or more, which reach the middle of the eye if bent forward. Charcoal grey to black or light brown above, cream or white below. Scaly tail much longer than head and body. Size range on that page: body 165-205 mm, tail 185-255 mm, weight 95-340 g. The museum's 'Is it a rat?' page says the tail longer than the body is the easy mark, and that no other rat has a tail longer than the body. Bush rats can equal body length but not exceed it. Brown rats have a shorter, thicker tail and a blunter snout. Climbing, daytime activity around people, and a nest of shredded paper in a roof point to the black rat, which is also called the roof rat. health.vic calls the same species the roof rat or ship rat: head and body 14-20 cm, tail about 25 cm, weight 200-300 g, pointed nose, large thin ears, spindle-shaped droppings. The two measurement sets are not identical. Both are cited rather than averaged. A native swamp rat has one ALA record inside 10 km of Inverleigh and none inside 5 km. Coat colour is a poor field mark. identification: Australian Museum: body 60-100 mm, tail 75-100 mm, weight 10-25 g. One pair of yellow chisel incisors, bulging eyes, large rounded ears, brownish-grey above and white to grey or pale yellow below, tail about the same length as the body. health.vic, under the name Mus domesticus: head and body 8-10 cm, tail 8-10 cm, weight 14-20 g, small spindle or irregular droppings. Agriculture Victoria: mainly active at night, using the same paths, able to jump at least 300 mm up and 2.5 m down, and to squeeze through an 8 mm gap. Adults eat about 3-5 g a day. They can live without free water if food is at least 15 percent moisture. Sources: https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/house-mouse/ ; https://www.health.vic.gov.au/environmental-health/rodents-pest-control ; https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/biosecurity/pest-animals/established-pest-animal-species/house-mouse (page last updated 22 Jul 2026).
origins: Agriculture Victoria: Mus musculus is an introduced species in Australia. At low density, mice live on native-grass and weed seeds and stay in refuge areas. Stubble retention and annual cropping add habitat. Breeding in the field generally runs from early spring until late autumn, and longer in buildings or haystacks. Numbers can reach plague levels when food, soil and moisture line up. The Australian Museum says the house mouse is found throughout Australia and sometimes in plague numbers, can breed at two months, and has litters of four to eight. Populations can rise about 18 months after fire while native rodents are low. No Inverleigh introduction date was found. Sources: https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/biosecurity/pest-animals/established-pest-animal-species/house-mouse ; https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/house-mouse/.
impacts: Agriculture Victoria: household and farm damage includes fouled food, chewed insulation, wiring and vehicle parts, seed dug up after sowing, seedlings eaten, and stem nodes gnawed so that seed heads fall. Losses up to 30 percent have been reported in maturing wheat, oats, barley, pulses, sorghum and maize. Vineyards and vegetables are also named. The monitoring rule of thumb on that page is that about 200 mice per hectare can cause significant damage and eat about as much as one sheep, and that 1,000 per hectare could eat 5 percent of freshly sown seed in a night. Those thresholds are not local densities. The Inverleigh Elliott-trap tally of 11 is not a per-hectare figure. Predators in south-eastern Australia, on that page, are falcons, owls, kites, kestrels, hawks, kookaburras, foxes, feral cats and snakes, and during a plague also butcherbirds, magpies, crows and ibis. Mice can transmit disease to people and livestock, and their mites can cause a rash. Handle dead mice with gloves or a tool. No Inverleigh plague or crop-loss study was found. Source: https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/biosecurity/pest-animals/established-pest-animal-species/house-mouse.

identification: Agriculture Victoria: feral cats (Felis catus) are hard to tell from domestic cats. Adult males commonly 3.4-6.4 kg (average 4.5), females 2.4-4.4 kg (average 3.2). The usual coat is striped tabby. Blotched tabby and black are common, and ginger or grey also occur. Persian or Siamese-type traits are not found in feral populations. Mostly solitary, most active around sunrise and sunset, and sheltering by day in rabbit burrows, hollow logs or dense scrub. In Victoria, home ranges are given as under 1 km2 up to 10 km2 when food is scarce, with males usually ranging further. The five local records do not say which of these coats or which ownership class was seen. Source: https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/biosecurity/pest-animals/established-pest-animal-species/cat-feral-or-wild.
origins: Origin on the Agriculture Victoria page: Europe, Africa and Asia. Cats may have reached Australia as early as the 17th century. European settlers brought them as pets in the late 18th century, and people deliberately released them in the 19th century to control rabbits and mice. They now occur over much of Australia, including most Victorian habitats and several offshore islands. Highest densities are described on small islands and in human-modified places such as farms and rubbish tips. No Inverleigh release story was found. Source: https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/biosecurity/pest-animals/established-pest-animal-species/cat-feral-or-wild.
impacts: Agriculture Victoria: feral cats hunt the most available prey and some individuals specialise. In Victoria, wild rabbits are a major food, and mice, smaller native mammals, reptiles, birds and invertebrates are also common. They scavenge when live prey is scarce. The page says feral cats are implicated in the extinction of 25 native small and medium mammal species and threaten more than 100 other native species. Annual predation estimates given there are 272 million birds, 470 million reptiles and 815 million mammals in Australia, plus unquantified invertebrates and amphibians. Cat-dependent disease costs on that page, covering feral and domestic cats, are AU$7.67-18.3 million a year in livestock losses from toxoplasmosis and sarcocystosis, and a potential AU$2.11-10.7 billion a year in human-health effects from toxoplasmosis and cat scratch disease. These are national ranges, not Golden Plains figures. Golden Plains Shire says most cat-nuisance complaints across the shire relate to feral cat populations, and that cats in town also fight, scratch furniture, disturb pets and kill native wildlife. The shire page also says 'In Victoria it's believed there are 500,000 unowned stray and feral cats' and that about 50,000 cats are impounded each year. That page does not cite the study behind those two numbers. There is no local diet study. The only reserve record with a method is a 2012 camera row at Bannockburn Bushland Reserve. Sources: https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/biosecurity/pest-animals/established-pest-animal-species/cat-feral-or-wild ; https://www.goldenplains.vic.gov.au/property-planning/pets-and-animals/cats.
legalStatus: Feral or wild cats are declared established pest animals only on specified Crown land, from 26 July 2018, under the Catchment and Land Protection Act 1994. The declaration applies to Crown land managed by DEECA, Parks Victoria, Phillip Island Nature Park and the four Alpine Resort Management Boards. They are not declared established pest animals on private land, so farmers and other private landholders are not required to control them there. The established-invasive-animals page repeats 'feral cats (on Crown land only)'. Farmers may manage feral cats among confined animals or near tethered animals under section 30 of the Domestic Animals Act 1994. Agriculture Victoria says a method that immediately kills the cat can be suitable if it is humane and safe. This note does not describe that method. Other landholders may cage-trap a cat found trespassing more than once, under current law, and must hand any trapped cat to the local council so it can be scanned and returned to an owner. Unidentified cats go to a pound or shelter under the Code of Practice. Recreational hunting of pest animals on Crown land does not extend to feral cats, except accredited volunteers in Parks Victoria or DEECA programs. Domestic cats in Golden Plains Shire are a council matter under the Domestic Animals Act 1994 and the Domestic Animal Management Plan, not the CaLP pest list. Sources: https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/biosecurity/pest-animals/established-pest-animal-species/cat-feral-or-wild ; https://agriculture.vic.gov.au/biosecurity/pest-animals/invasive-animal-management/established-invasive-animals.

whatToDo: Golden Plains Shire does not have a cat curfew. The Domestic Animal Management Plan 2026-2029, adopted on 25 November 2025, says a cat curfew was requested in the 2021 consultation, officers found it was not achievable during the 2022-2025 plan, and it is not included in this plan. identification: iNaturalist taxon 42165 is Axis porcinus, preferred common name Indochinese Hog Deer. DEECA and the Game Management Authority use Hog Deer for the animal that is excepted from the private-land unprotection order. No Victorian field-description page was opened, and there is no local record to describe. Chital, Axis axis, was checked because the names are sometimes confused. Its ALA facet inside 50 km was also empty.
origins: Hog deer are one of the four deer species DEECA says are known in Victoria. They are wildlife under the Wildlife Act 1975, not a CaLP established pest. No release history was opened. No occurrence near Inverleigh, or within 50 km of the centre, was returned by ALA or iNaturalist.
impacts: The statewide deer-impact paragraph on the DEECA program page covers deer as a group. Hog deer are not the species named in the Flora and Fauna Guarantee potentially-threatening-process sentence, which is Sambar. There is no local impact record.
legalStatus: Deer are not established pest animals under the Catchment and Land Protection Act 1994. DEECA's Victorian Deer Control Program says the game classification under the Wildlife Act 1975 does not stop control when deer damage the environment or property, and that the National Parks Act 1975 requires managers to deal with introduced species in national parks, including deer. On private land, an Unprotection Order under section 7A of the Wildlife Act allows control of problem deer except Hog Deer by ground shooting, without an Authority to Control Wildlife, if the firearm meets the Order. The Order was not copied for calibres or projectile weights. Hog Deer, and any method other than ground shooting with a compliant firearm, including trapping, still need an Authority to Control Wildlife. On public land, a section 28G Authorisation Order (the PDF linked by DEECA is dated 16 October 2025) authorises public land managers, Victoria Police and registered veterinarians. The Game Management Authority fact sheet, page last updated 2 Jun 2021, says the same private-land unprotection for all deer species except Hog Deer, where they are causing damage, and says the Order was made for 10 years. The later DEECA page still describes that private-land rule and links the Order. The program says there are four known deer species in Victoria and that aerial and ground shooting target Sambar, Fallow and Red deer. Sambar is listed as a potentially threatening process under the Flora and Fauna Guarantee Act 1988 because it reduces the biodiversity of native vegetation. Deer damage described by DEECA is weeds, grazing, tree rubbing, trampling, wallows, soil erosion and extra grazing pressure on native wildlife. Adult Sambar weight is given as 100-350 kg. Sources: https://www.environment.vic.gov.au/invasive-plants-and-animals/deer-control-program ; https://www.gma.vic.gov.au/hunting/deer/where-to-hunt/fact-sheets/controlling-problem-deer-on-private-property. Hog Deer are the exception. They were not declared unprotected on private land. Destroying Hog Deer, on land that is not managed under the National Parks Act, needs an Authority to Control Wildlife. Trapping any deer without that authority is an offence.
hangouts: No Hog Deer row inside 5, 10, 25 or 50 km on ALA, and none inside 50 km on iNaturalist taxon 42165. No locality string in the deer facets names Inverleigh. There is no hangout to list. The nearest deer of any species in these pulls are fallow deer about 24 km south (ALA) and a casual fallow deer at Anakie about 24.7 km north (iNaturalist), plus one Sambar at 25.1 km. None of those is a hog deer and none is Inverleigh.
whatToDo: Do not treat a deer as a CaLP pest or as a rabbit-style landowner duty. There is no Inverleigh or 10 km record of this species in the ALA or iNaturalist pulls, so there is no local hangout to bait or to clear. Absence of records is not proof that a deer has never crossed the district. If one is seen, the useful act is a photograph and a report with a precise place, through iNaturalist or the land manager, so the gap in the public record can close. A FeralScan deer-recording page was not opened in this pass, so its form is not described. The rabbit, fox, cat and mouse FeralScan datasets are a different set of products. On private land the legal path for problem deer other than Hog Deer is the section 7A Order, read on the DEECA and Game Management Authority pages, including the firearm conditions in the Order and the Firearms Act 1996. Those conditions are not reprinted here. Hog Deer still needs an Authority to Control Wildlife from the Conservation Regulator. Trapping is an offence unless that authority is issued. Public-land control is for the land manager under the section 28G authorisation, not a general public permit. If the animal might be a Hog Deer, do not use the private-land unprotection order. The order excludes Hog Deer, and an Authority to Control Wildlife is required.
